memories.content: Calculate user study compensation budgets based on estimated participation burden, combining session time and preparation effort.
Compensate for required travel time in face-to-face user studies as well.
Compensate for the actual time participants spent in sessions, regardless of research modality.
Leave cash payment as an available compensation method for face-to-face studies.
If compensation equity is explained, do not require finalizing the payment method at the proposal stage.
Apply the same base hourly rate to face-to-face and remote studies if task burden is equal.
Participants judge compensation fairness based on the total burden, combining session time with required travel and preparation time.
Account in compensation for the burden of rescheduling iterations and returning for multiple formative evaluation sessions.
Compensate participants for time already invested even if a session is terminated early due to prototype errors.
The author of this proposal tends to exclude preparation burden between sessions when calculating compensation for iterative studies.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Allow the problem framing to extend through a third sentence when a concrete person, setting, or use situation is needed to make the issue understandable.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Use the third sentence for the specific setting and consequence rather than compressing them into an abstract two-sentence summary.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Explicitly specify the users, operational stakeholders, and actual usage environment in the primary HCI research question.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Provide one compact visual summary when proposing an unfamiliar interaction procedure.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Mark the conditions that move an unfamiliar interaction procedure from one step to the next in its visual summary.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Present the master’s research schedule as phase-specific milestones for field understanding, system implementation, user study, and analysis.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Link deliverables that determine entry into the next phase to each milestone of the master’s research.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Directly connect the gap in the actual usage context with the proposed design and operational contributions in a single flow.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Avoid extra subheadings in a two-page proposal; use paragraph transitions to preserve one continuous argument from problem to proposed response and next steps.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Begin each paragraph by connecting it to the previous claim so the short proposal reads as an argument rather than a stack of labeled fragments.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Place preliminary results from field observations or technical validations near sentences supporting feasibility claims.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Readers may misinterpret a compressed opening when the person, setting, or consequence is only implied.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] A two-sentence opening can become so general that readers understand the topic but cannot picture the situation the proposal intends to change.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Use paragraph transitions instead of extra headings when the repeated labels would consume space needed for the argument itself.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] End each paragraph with the question or consequence that the next paragraph answers.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] A continuous sequence of problem, consequence, response, and next step makes the relationship among claims audible without repeating section labels.
[task-2/advisor2/structure] Readers may experience very short headed sections as an outline because each new label interrupts the connection to the previous paragraph.
[task-2/advisor2/emphasis] Do not exceed two primary HCI contributions that readers must remember.
[task-2/advisor2/emphasis] Present each design or operational contribution as a single named sentence.
[task-2/advisor2/emphasis] In studies recruiting organizational members, emphasize workflow constraints.
[task-2/advisor2/emphasis] In studies recruiting organizational members, emphasize manager approval constraints.
[task-2/advisor2/emphasis] HCI reviewers find it difficult to identify primary contributions when named design and operational contributions exceed two.
[task-2/advisor2/emphasis] Highlight one primary field operational decision to be changed by evaluation results as the central claim.
[task-2/advisor2/emphasis] Specify prototype features unnecessary for reviewing the primary field problem as secondary scope.
[task-2/advisor2/style] Use an em dash only for a deliberate interruption or sharp contrast; otherwise split the sentence or choose ordinary punctuation.
[task-2/advisor2/style] In procedural passages, begin each sentence with the action, condition, or output instead of repeating “we” so the steps remain easy to follow and reuse.
[task-2/advisor2/style] Write system behaviors confirmed in the actual usage environment as observed states.
[task-2/advisor2/style] Write system behaviors not yet confirmed in the field as conditional plans.
[task-2/advisor2/style] Readers can reconstruct a sequence more accurately when each sentence begins with the action or condition rather than the author.
[task-2/advisor2/style] Do not mechanically split connected thoughts into separate short sentences when doing so destroys the intended reading rhythm.
[task-2/advisor2/style] Preserve a longer sentence when its clauses form one continuous movement that is easier to follow together than apart.
[task-2/advisor2/style] The user understands that short sentences are easier to scan but feels that uniformly segmented prose loses its reading rhythm.
[task-2/advisor2/style] Write procedural sentences so their opening phrase can be reused as a checklist item without changing the step's meaning.
[task-2/advisor2/style] The user should choose “I” as an individual author or “we” for a named team and should not mix them when describing the same responsible party.
[task-2/advisor2/style] Action-first procedural sentences can be reordered or copied into a checklist more easily because their subject is the step rather than the proposal author.
[task-2/advisor2/style] The user can explain whether an em dash marks an intentional interruption or contrast rather than using it decoratively.
[task-2/advisor2/style] An em dash creates a stronger interruption than a comma and can make a deliberate contrast easier to hear in the sentence.
[task-2/advisor2/claim-evidence] Place observational evidence or sources adjacent to claims regarding user needs or field effects.
[task-2/advisor2/claim-evidence] Distinguish at the sentence level between facts already confirmed in the field and predictions to be examined in the user study.
[task-2/advisor2/claim-evidence] Do not use verbs implying proof of causality if the design does not support causal inference.
[task-2/advisor2/claim-evidence] Prioritize citations of recent systems and field research in rapidly changing HCI topics.
[task-2/advisor2/claim-evidence] Explain the user or operational stakeholder needs that each design choice aims to address.
[task-2/advisor2/claim-evidence] Support each important conclusion with the closest evidence that directly examined it.
[task-2/advisor2/claim-evidence] Reviewers first check direct evidence placed closest to important conclusions.
[task-2/advisor2/claim-evidence] Use field cases in which people completed tasks by working around existing tools as evidence for the need for the design.
[task-2/advisor2/claim-evidence] Distinguish between problems reported by operational stakeholders and those directly observed by the researcher as separate forms of evidence.
[task-2/advisor2/claim-evidence] Field breakdown logs can reveal both system failures and user adaptive behaviors, including their timing and conditions.

[task-2/advisor2/claim-evidence] In field sites introducing new systems, formal procedures often coexist with existing manual routines for a period, making it difficult to isolate the effects of single design changes.
[task-2/advisor2/expression] Use a sequence table rather than a flow diagram when the procedure is likely to change repeatedly during drafting.
[task-2/advisor2/expression] The visual fidelity of a prototype and its level of connection to actual data and services may differ.
[task-2/advisor2/expression] Service flow diagrams indicate human-system transitions that are not revealed by individual screens alone.
[task-2/advisor2/expression] HCI reviewers often scan system structure and service flow diagrams before the main text.
[task-2/advisor2/expression] Give each step, actor, condition, and outcome a stable row in the sequence table.
[task-2/advisor2/expression] Updating one row in a sequence table is usually faster than redrawing a branching diagram after a procedural change.
[task-2/advisor2/expression] Readers can check sequence tables step by step but may find the overall branching shape less immediate.
[task-2/advisor2/terminology] Do not change names referring to the same user roles, system functions, or operational stages midway.
[task-2/advisor2/terminology] Use abbreviations only for long recurring terms in a two-page proposal.
[task-2/advisor2/terminology] Present the full term and abbreviation together when using an abbreviation for the first time.
[task-2/advisor2/terminology] Refer to participants based on the roles they perform in the study rather than their status.
[task-2/advisor2/terminology] Reviewers from different subfields find it difficult to infer an abbreviation from context alone when it is not defined at first use.
[task-2/advisor2/terminology] When introducing an operational role for the first time, define both the decisions it can make and the actions it performs.
[task-2/advisor2/terminology] Individuals holding identical job titles may possess different system modification privileges and data access rights depending on their deployment site.
[task-2/advisor2/terminology] The user tends to group distinct field roles under the single label “user.”
[task-2/advisor2/methods] Specify field and user data sources and analysis procedures corresponding to all HCI research questions.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] In preregistered studies, clarify the criteria for judging plan changes.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] In preregistered studies, clarify the location for recording plan changes.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] Use a justified minimum-to-maximum target range when confirmations can change, and tie the minimum and maximum to different workload and budget cases.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] Specify the observation records, system logs, or interview tools used to collect each type of field and user data.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] Specify whether each type of field and user data will be collected before, during, or after deployment.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] Readers cannot assess a target range unless both bounds have a stated consequence for schedule, workload, or cost.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] In field deployments, network and service instability exist as independent causes of task failure alongside design choices.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] If a safety signal occurs in the field system, existing institutional safety procedures take precedence over the research schedule and data collection plan.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] Reviewers judge answerability by tracing the path from each research question to its data sources and analysis procedures.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] The user authoring this proposal tends to present implemented feature lists directly as design contributions.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] Define what can still be completed at the minimum target instead of treating every number inside the range as operationally identical.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] Use a bounded range to absorb expected confirmation changes without pretending that one early estimate is guaranteed.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] Show how session count and facilitator time change at the minimum and maximum bounds.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] Define the additional workload or deliverable enabled at the maximum target so the upper bound is not an arbitrary cushion.
[task-2/advisor2/methods] A bounded range preserves uncertainty honestly but makes the final workload and budget less certain than one fixed target.
[task-2/advisor2/evaluation] Specify a single representative measure that will drive operational decisions to maintain, modify, or discontinue the deployed design.
[task-2/advisor2/evaluation] The HCI review panel verifies whether operational decisions can be made based on the declared primary measure.
[task-2/advisor2/evaluation] Establish decision thresholds indicating at what levels key metrics trigger maintaining, modifying, or discontinuing the design.
[task-2/advisor2/evaluation] Evaluate whether reducing workload for one role creates new tasks for other roles through the proposed design changes.
[task-2/advisor2/evaluation] Distinguish usability from organizational adoption intent as separate evaluation outcomes.
[task-2/advisor2/evaluation] Implementation fidelity indicates whether planned features and operational procedures were delivered in the field according to intended specifications.
[task-2/advisor2/evaluation] Initial evaluations and long-term operation do not share identical measurement conditions due to differences in system exposure duration and frequency of repeated use.
[task-2/advisor2/ethics] Link anticipated participant burden with its mitigation strategies for each field user study task.
[task-2/advisor2/ethics] Specify the accommodations necessary for participants to access the field system and research tasks.
[task-2/advisor2/ethics] Specify how accessibility accommodations will be provided in the field user study.
[task-2/advisor2/ethics] Describe how personal identifiers will be separated from research data immediately upon collection.
[task-2/advisor2/ethics] List equipment to be loaned when participants lack necessary gear.
[task-2/advisor2/ethics] Describe the procedure for returning equipment loaned to participants.
[task-2/advisor2/ethics] The HCI ethics reviewer verifies that anticipated burden and mitigation strategies correspond for each field user study task.
[task-2/advisor2/ethics] Ensure that participants can safely return to existing work procedures if they discontinue research participation.
[task-2/advisor2/ethics] Specify that organizational members who decline research participation will not face disadvantages in task assignment or performance evaluation.
[task-2/advisor2/ethics] The user's withdrawal risk can be adequately assessed only when a safe alternative procedure exists for field tasks.
[task-2/advisor2/ethics] The user tends to assume that a short session also entails little burden from work interruption and exposure to a manager.
[task-2/advisor2/scope] Specify in one sentence the user population and actual usage environment to which the design knowledge applies.
[task-2/advisor2/scope] Reviewers judge the generalization boundary of results through the specified target population and environment.
[task-2/advisor2/scope] Specify the workflow, technical infrastructure, and operational-authority conditions that must match before applying the design guidelines at another field site.
[task-2/advisor2/scope] The transferability of field design knowledge depends not only on user characteristics but also on workflow and technological–organizational infrastructure.
[task-2/advisor2/scope] The user tends to apply results confirmed at one deployment site to all similar organizations.
[task-2/advisor2/safety] List whom to notify and in what order if serious discomfort is reported during the study.
[task-2/advisor2/safety] Field staff rely on the pre-defined contact sequence when serious discomfort is reported.
[task-2/advisor2/safety] Define the thresholds for participant harm, operational disruption, and data anomalies at which deployment and data collection must cease.
[task-2/advisor2/safety] Establish procedures to restore existing systems and workflow states after suspending field deployment.
[task-2/advisor2/safety] The user's stop plan can be judged feasible only when it identifies who has authority to order recovery and who is responsible for carrying it out.

[task-2/advisor2/safety] In organizations where error reporting is linked to individual performance evaluations, safety signal records may be separated from research decision logs, potentially breaking the traceability path for the same incident.
[task-2/advisor2/feasibility] Mark unverified schedule assumptions as such.
[task-2/advisor2/feasibility] Mark unverified recruitment assumptions as such.
[task-2/advisor2/feasibility] Mark unverified technical assumptions as such.
[task-2/advisor2/feasibility] Trace back the resources required for each core prototype feature and field research procedure.
[task-2/advisor2/feasibility] Operations reviewers judge feasibility by examining the personnel required for each procedure.
[task-2/advisor2/feasibility] Operations reviewers judge feasibility by examining the equipment required for each procedure.
[task-2/advisor2/feasibility] Operations reviewers judge feasibility by examining the time required for each procedure.
[task-2/advisor2/feasibility] Document separately the commitments and confirmation status of field partners required for recruitment, installation, and operational support.
[task-2/advisor2/feasibility] Designate a responsible party for software updates, equipment inspections, and user support during the deployment period.
[task-2/advisor2/feasibility] The user's deployment readiness can be assessed only when dependencies on external services and field personnel are visible.
[task-2/advisor2/feasibility] Field schedules and assigned personnel may change due to operational factors beyond the researcher’s control.
[task-2/advisor2/reproducibility] HCI reviewers find it difficult to assess result reproducibility if the system version used in the field deployment is not disclosed.
[task-2/advisor2/reproducibility] Record changes in system configurations, field procedures, and data collection tools during deployment, along with their timestamps and rationales.
[task-2/advisor2/reproducibility] The history of deployment versions and configuration changes provides necessary evidence for interpreting results from different field sites.
[task-2/advisor2/budget] Keep the main text to the total and major categories, and place quantities, unit rates, and assumptions in one compact budget table or appendix.
[task-2/advisor2/budget] Give each cost category, quantity, unit rate, and subtotal a stable row in the separate budget table.
[task-2/advisor2/budget] Put the estimate basis in a dedicated table column so one assumption can be checked or revised without rewriting the narrative.
[task-2/advisor2/budget] Readers can verify arithmetic and compare categories faster in a consistent table than in amounts distributed across prose.
[task-2/advisor2/budget] Revise one table row and its subtotal when an estimate changes instead of repeating the new amount across several prose paragraphs.
[task-2/advisor2/budget] Keep detailed arithmetic out of the main argument when readers can reach the complete table from a clear reference.
[task-2/advisor2/budget] The user tends to interrupt the argument with long cost enumerations when no separate budget table is available.
[task-2/advisor2/compensation] Calculate user research compensation budgets based on the estimated participation burden, combining session time with required technical and travel preparation.
[task-2/advisor2/compensation] Compensate participants who withdraw from the study midway for their actual participation time.
[task-2/advisor2/compensation] Compensate for the time actually spent in sessions, regardless of the research modality.
[task-2/advisor2/compensation] Allow the issuance of gift cards of equivalent value to participants in remote studies who cannot use electronic transfers.
[task-2/advisor2/compensation] Do not treat an unresolved payment method as a deficiency at the proposal stage.
[task-2/advisor2/compensation] Allow differential compensation amounts for on-site and remote studies when participation burden varies due to travel or technical preparation.
[task-2/advisor2/compensation] Participants judge the fairness of compensation based on the combined burden of session time and required technical and travel preparation.
[task-2/advisor2/compensation] In longitudinal studies requiring diary entries and repeated reporting, include out-of-session recording time in compensation calculations.
[task-2/advisor2/compensation] Distinguish between participant research compensation and labor costs for field staff performing installation and operational support as part of their duties.
[task-2/advisor2/compensation] The user tends to count session time but omit participants’ advance setup and follow-up reporting time.
[task-2/advisor2/review] Conduct one review prior to submission focusing solely on the validity of user problems, system interventions, and field evaluation logic.
[task-2/advisor2/review] Cross-check whether research questions align with the core functions of the system.
[task-2/advisor2/review] Cross-check whether field tasks align with representative measures.
[task-2/advisor2/review] Cross-check whether the evidence to be collected aligns with the design and operational decisions to be changed.
[task-2/advisor2/review] Finally verify that the user problem, system intervention, field evaluation, and expected contribution form one coherent logical flow.
[task-2/advisor2/review] HCI reviewers view the validity of design interventions as low if research questions do not connect to system functions.
[task-2/advisor2/review] HCI reviewers view the validity of evaluation plans as low if field tasks fail to generate representative measures.
[task-2/advisor2/review] HCI reviewers view the practical utility of contributions as low if collected evidence cannot change design or operational decisions.
[task-2/advisor2/review] Before submission, conduct a sequential walkthrough with field liaisons of installation failures, operational interruptions, and recovery scenarios.
[task-2/advisor2/review] Verify in one sentence how each proposed contribution could actually alter specific design or operational decisions.
[task-2/advisor2/review] The user must distinguish unconfirmed field partners and equipment from finalized ones so remaining execution risks can be assessed.

analysis.overview: The frames overlap on burden-based compensation, actual session time, payment-method flexibility, fairness, and longitudinal or interrupted participation. Their differences are conditional rather than contradictory. The reference uniquely retains cash, while the compared frame adds extensive proposal, methods, ethics, feasibility, evaluation, and reporting guidance.

relations.reason: The reference splits travel from the general burden calculation, while the compared claim combines the same components.
relations.summary: Compensation budgets should include session time plus required preparation and travel burden.

relations.reason: Both frames state the same operational compensation rule under the same scope.
relations.summary: Actual session time should be compensated regardless of research modality.

relations.reason: Only the reference addresses retaining cash as an in-person payment option.
relations.summary: Cash should remain available for face-to-face studies.

relations.reason: Both allow proposal-stage flexibility, but the reference explicitly conditions it on explaining equity while the compared statement does not.
relations.summary: An unresolved payment method need not be finalized at proposal time when compensation equity is explained.

relations.reason: The explicit equal-burden and unequal-burden conditions explain and preserve the different rate instructions.
relations.summary: On-site and remote compensation should share a base rate when burdens are equal and may differ when travel or technical preparation changes burden.

relations.reason: Both frames express the same fairness claim, with the compared wording specifying technical preparation.
relations.summary: Participants assess compensation fairness from combined session, preparation, and travel burden.

relations.reason: Rescheduling, return visits, diary entries, and repeated reporting are complementary forms of additional longitudinal burden.
relations.summary: Compensation calculations should include burdens created outside individual sessions in repeated or longitudinal studies.

relations.reason: The shared rule applies under different explicit circumstances: prototype-error termination and participant withdrawal.
relations.summary: Participants should be paid for actual time already invested when participation ends early.

relations.reason: The frames describe complementary manifestations of the same budgeting omission across iterative and broader study contexts.
relations.summary: The proposal author tends to omit compensable preparation or follow-up work outside sessions.
